items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "positive inductive effect"?
options: An amine with one alkyl or aryl group on the nitrogen atom, RNH₂.
An organic compound derived from ammonia by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms with alkyl or aryl groups.
The donation of electron density by alkyl groups, which increases the availability of the nitrogen lone pair.
C₆H₅NH₂, an aromatic amine made by reducing nitrobenzene with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: The donation of electron density by alkyl groups, which increases the availability of the nitrogen lone pair.
items.markingKey: Positive inductive effect: the donation of electron density by alkyl groups, which increases the availability of the nitrogen lone pair.

items.stem: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?
options: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept H⁺
The ring donates electrons to nitrogen
items.answer: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept H⁺
items.markingKey: Overlap with π system.

items.stem: Why does the reaction of bromoethane with ammonia give a mixture of products?

items.answer: The ethylamine formed is itself a nucleophile and reacts with more bromoethane
items.markingKey: Further substitution gives secondary and tertiary amines.

items.stem: pKa values of the conjugate acids: phenylamine 4.6; propylamine 10.57; ethylamine 10.73; ammonia 9.25. Which is the strongest base?
items.answer: Ethylamine

Kenji compares the basicity of ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine. pKa values of the conjugate acids: NH₄⁺ 9.25, CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ 10.73, C₆H₅NH₃⁺ 4.60. (a) Use the data to place the three bases in order of increasing strength and explain the order. (b) Explain why the product mixture is made alkaline with NaOH after reduction.
items.answer: (a) Phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine; ethyl group donates electron density (lone pair more available); in phenylamine lone pair delocalised into ring (less available). (b) In acid the amine is present as the phenylammonium salt; NaOH releases the free amine.
items.markingKey: (a) order [1]; ethylamine [1]; phenylamine [1] [3] (b) In acid the amine is present as the phenylammonium salt; NaOH releases the free amine [1]

(a) Use the data to place the three bases in order of increasing strength and explain the order. (b) Describe how phenylamine is made from benzene in two steps.
items.answer: (a) Phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine; ethyl group donates electron density (lone pair more available); in phenylamine lone pair delocalised into ring (less available). (b) Nitration (conc HNO₃/H₂SO₄, < 55 °C) to nitrobenzene; reduction with Sn/conc HCl under reflux, then NaOH.

items.answer: Phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine

items.stem: Explain why ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
items.answer: The ethyl group donates electron density to the nitrogen (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept a proton.

items.stem: Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia.
items.answer: The lone pair on nitrogen overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring, spreading the electron density and making the lone pair less available to accept H⁺.
items.markingKey: lone pair delocalised into ring [1]; less available [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why excess ammonia is used to make a primary amine from a halogenoalkane.
items.answer: To make it more likely that the halogenoalkane reacts with ammonia rather than with the amine product, reducing the formation of secondary and tertiary amines and quaternary salts.
items.markingKey: To make it more likely that the halogenoalkane reacts with ammonia rather than with the amine product [1]; reducing the formation of secondary and tertiary amines and quaternary salts [1] [2]

items.stem: Why must diazotisation be carried out below 10 °C?

items.stem: Why are azo compounds coloured?

The N=N bond is very weak
items.answer: The –N=N– group extends the delocalised π system across both rings, so visible light is absorbed

items.stem: Describe how phenylamine could be converted into an azo dye by coupling with phenol. Give the reagents and conditions for each stage and the structure of the dye.
items.answer: Stage 1: NaNO₂ and dilute HCl below 10 °C forms benzenediazonium chloride, C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻. Stage 2: add to phenol in alkaline solution (NaOH) (cold): C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄OH, a yellow-orange azo dye.

items.stem: A dye company in Mumbai makes an azo dye from benzene in four steps, via nitrobenzene, then phenylamine derivative 4-methylphenylamine, then 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride, which is coupled with phenol. (a) Give the reagents and conditions for converting benzene into nitrobenzene and then into phenylamine. (b) Explain why the dye is coloured.
items.answer: (a) Conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄ below 55 °C; then Sn + conc HCl, reflux, then NaOH(aq). (b) The –N=N– group links two aromatic rings into an extended delocalised system that absorbs light in the visible region.
items.markingKey: (a) nitration [1]; reduction [1] [2] (b) The –N=N– group links two aromatic rings into an extended delocalised system that absorbs light in the visible region [2] [2]

items.stem: Explain why benzenediazonium ions act as electrophiles in coupling reactions.
items.answer: The terminal nitrogen of –N₂⁺ is electron-deficient (positive charge) and accepts a pair of electrons from the activated ring of phenol, forming an –N=N– link by electrophilic substitution.

items.stem: Explain why aryl diazonium salts are more stable than alkyl diazonium salts.
items.answer: The positive charge of the –N₂⁺ group is partly delocalised into the benzene ring, stabilising it; alkyl diazonium ions decompose immediately even at low temperature.
items.markingKey: The positive charge of the –N₂⁺ group is partly delocalised into the benzene ring, stabilising it [1]; alkyl diazonium ions decompose immediately even at low temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why azo dyes made from different amines and coupling agents have different colours.

items.answer: Stage 1: NaNO₂ and dilute HCl below 10 °C forms 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride, CH₃C₆H₄N₂⁺Cl⁻. Stage 2: add to phenol in alkaline solution (NaOH) (cold): CH₃C₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₄OH, a yellow-orange azo dye.
items.markingKey: NaNO₂ + HCl [1]; below 10 °C [1]; diazonium salt [1]; coupling conditions [1]; azo product structure [1] [5]

items.stem: A dye company in Singapore makes an azo dye from benzene in four steps, via nitrobenzene, then phenylamine derivative 4-nitrophenylamine, then 4-nitrobenzenediazonium chloride, which is coupled with naphthalen-2-ol. (a) Write an equation for the diazotisation and explain why the temperature must be kept low. (b) Explain why the dye is coloured. (c) State what is formed if the diazonium solution is warmed with water.
items.answer: (a) O₂NC₆H₄NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → O₂NC₆H₄N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O; below 10 °C as the diazonium salt decomposes above this. (b) The –N=N– group links two aromatic rings into an extended delocalised system that absorbs light in the visible region. (c) A phenol (and N₂ gas, H⁺).
items.markingKey: (a) equation [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) The –N=N– group links two aromatic rings into an extended delocalised system that absorbs light in the visible region [2] [2] (c) A phenol (and N₂ gas, H⁺) [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "reduction of an amide"?
options: The –CONH– linkage that joins amino acids in proteins and monomers in polyamides.
A compound containing the –CONH– group (–CONH₂ for primary amides), e.g. ethanamide CH₃CONH₂.
The conversion of an amide into an amine with LiAlH₄ in dry ether, e.g. CH₃CONH₂ → CH₃CH₂NH₂.
LiAlH₄, a powerful reducing agent used in dry ether to reduce amides and nitriles to amines.
items.answer: The conversion of an amide into an amine with LiAlH₄ in dry ether, e.g. CH₃CONH₂ → CH₃CH₂NH₂.
items.markingKey: Reduction of an amide: the conversion of an amide into an amine with LiAlH₄ in dry ether, e.g. CH₃CONH₂ → CH₃CH₂NH₂.

items.stem: A student in Kathmandu states: "Amides are basic like amines because they contain an NH₂ group." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Amides are almost neutral because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the C=O group.

items.stem: Chloe prepares N-phenylethanamide, CH₃CONHC₆H₅, from ethanoyl chloride and phenylamine, and then investigates its reactions. (a) Write an equation for the formation of the amide. (b) Give the products of hydrolysis of the amide with hot dilute acid and with hot aqueous alkali. (c) Give the reagent for reducing the amide and name the product.
items.answer: (a) CH₃COCl + 2C₆H₅NH₂ → CH₃CONHC₆H₅ + C₆H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻ (b) acid: ethanoic acid + phenylamine as its salt; alkali: the ethanoate salt + phenylamine (c) LiAlH₄ in dry ether; N-ethylphenylamine (CH₃CH₂NHC₆H₅)

items.stem: Explain why amino acids are soluble in water but insoluble in non-polar solvents.
items.answer: Zwitterions are ionic and form strong ion–dipole attractions with water; non-polar solvents cannot overcome the ionic attractions.

items.stem: Explain why the hydrolysis of a protein gives a mixture of amino acids.
items.answer: Heating with 6 mol dm⁻³ HCl breaks the peptide (amide) bonds, releasing the individual amino acids that made up the chain.

items.stem: Priya compares the basicity of ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine. pKa values of the conjugate acids: NH₄⁺ 9.25, CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ 10.73, C₆H₅NH₃⁺ 4.60. (a) Write an equation to show ethylamine acting as a base in water. (b) Use the data to place the three bases in order of increasing strength and explain the order. (c) Describe how phenylamine is made from benzene in two steps. (d) Explain why the product mixture is made alkaline with NaOH after reduction.
items.answer: (a) CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ (b) Phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine; ethyl group donates electron density (lone pair more available); in phenylamine lone pair delocalised into ring (less available). (c) Nitration (conc HNO₃/H₂SO₄, < 55 °C) to nitrobenzene; reduction with Sn/conc HCl under reflux, then NaOH. (d) In acid the amine is present as the phenylammonium salt; NaOH releases the free amine.
items.markingKey: (a) CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ [1] (b) order [1]; ethylamine [1]; phenylamine [1] [3] (c) step 1 [1]; step 2 [1] [2] (d) In acid the amine is present as the phenylammonium salt; NaOH releases the free amine [1]

items.stem: Ethan hydrolyses a tripeptide and separates the products by electrophoresis at pH 7. The amino acids are aspartic acid (pI 2.77), serine (pI 5.68) and lysine (pI 9.74). (a) Predict the direction of movement of each amino acid. (b) Explain why the isoelectric point of aspartic acid is very different from that of glycine (5.97). (c) Explain how the spots are located and identified after electrophoresis. (d) State how many different tripeptides could contain these three amino acids, each once.
items.answer: (a) aspartic acid: to anode; serine: to anode; lysine: to cathode (b) Its side chain (CH₂COOH) contains an extra acidic –COOH group, which loses H⁺, so a lower pH is needed for no overall charge. (c) Spray with ninhydrin (purple spots) or use UV; compare distances with known standards run under the same conditions. (d) 6 (3! sequences)
